post.body:
Moving To Northern Colorado — The Honest Version

People find this page because they're weighing a move to Northern Colorado — usually from out of state, sometimes from Denver metro, occasionally from the mountains looking for a lower-elevation base. The pitch is easy: mountain views, real seasons, a working economy, and towns that still know each other. The harder part is figuring out which town.

Roughly the hardest thing about moving here isn't finding a house — it's working out which of thirty-odd towns you want to wake up in, from a thousand miles away, on the strength of a weekend visit. This page is the short version of that answer. The full version — every town side-by-side, schools, drive times, what's being built, and what homes actually cost — is in the free relocation guide.

What "Northern Colorado" Actually Means

For the purposes of this site, Northern Colorado (NoCo) is Larimer and Weld counties plus the northern edge of Boulder County — the corridor along I-25 from north of Denver up to the Wyoming border, and the Front Range foothills that flank it. The anchor cities are Fort Collins (population 175,000, home of Colorado State University) and Greeley (population 110,000, home of UNC and the region's agricultural core). Everything else is smaller — and often better for what people are actually looking for when they move here.

Loveland — The Base I Recommend Most

Loveland sits between Fort Collins and Longmont with real lakes (Boyd Lake, Lake Loveland), a genuinely walkable downtown, and access to both Rocky Mountain National Park (45 minutes) and Denver International (80 minutes). Median home price in mid-2026 is running around $525K. The public schools (Thompson School District) are strong. It's the town I chose when I left, then came back to. Bias acknowledged.

Fort Collins — If You Want The College Town

CSU drives the culture, the biking infrastructure is real, and Old Town Fort Collins is one of the best small downtowns in the West. It's also the priciest NoCo option — median above $600K for anything close to the core — and traffic on College Avenue has grown into something that would've been unimaginable ten years ago. Great town, no longer a small town.

Windsor — The Suburb That Grew Up

Between Fort Collins and Greeley, Windsor has doubled in population in fifteen years and has the newest inventory of the main NoCo towns. Good for buyers who want new construction, HOA amenities, and a shorter drive to both DIA and Denver's tech corridor. Less good for buyers who want old bones, mature trees, and character.

Berthoud — Small Town, Growing Fast

Twelve miles south of Loveland with genuinely rural feel on its edges, Berthoud is the town most likely to surprise you on a scouting trip. Solid schools, a real downtown, and prices that still start with a "4" for a lot of homes. The catch: new construction is arriving quickly, and the "small-town character" everyone wants is being tested by how many people are choosing it.

Wellington, Ault, Pierce, Nunn — The Rural Belt

North and northeast of Fort Collins, these are the working farm-and-ranch towns. Wellington is the largest and closest — 15 minutes from Fort Collins on I-25 — and the median price point ($450K–$500K range) buys real house. Ault, Pierce, and Nunn get more rural and more agricultural the further out you go. These are the towns buyers move to when they want land, quiet, and a driveway their neighbors don't share.

Estes Park — The Mountain Base

The eastern gateway to Rocky Mountain National Park. Full-time Estes residents deal with weather, tourism seasonality, and a housing market shaped by short-term rentals as much as by year-round buyers. Beautiful and specific — not a general-audience recommendation. If you're weighing it, the questions to ask are about winter access, wildfire mitigation, and whether the local economy supports the work you plan to do.

Greeley — Underrated, Undervalued

Greeley carries an old reputation among Front Range transplants that no longer matches the actual town. It has a university, a real downtown, the lowest median home price of any major NoCo city (mid-$400s in mid-2026), and a working-community feel that Fort Collins and Windsor priced out years ago. Worth a genuine look, not a drive-through.

What This Region Isn't

It isn't a mountain town — the mountains are 30 to 60 minutes west of the I-25 corridor, and if that matters to you daily, look at Estes Park, Lyons, or the foothills subdivisions rather than the main NoCo cities. It isn't Boulder — the culture, price point, and politics are meaningfully different, and buyers coming from Boulder either love that difference or don't. And it isn't Denver — the drive to DIA is a real 75–90 minutes, and NoCo functions as its own economy rather than as a commuter suburb.

How To Actually Do This Move

The workable version is a scouting trip to choose the town, then a focused touring trip, with honest video walkthroughs in between. What you should not do is waive an inspection to win a bidding war on a house you have only seen on a screen — that mistake made a lot of 2021 buyers unhappy for the next three years, and the market corrected enough that it's no longer necessary.

If you're a veteran or active duty, VA loans are a meaningful and workable path in this market — a real share of the buyers I help are using them, and knowing how a VA-backed offer reads to a NoCo seller is part of the job.

What Christine Does For Relocation Clients

The [free Northern Colorado Relocation Guide](/relocation.html) covers every town side-by-side — schools, commute times, what's being built, and what homes actually cost.
